title: const declarations
summary: Declares a block-scoped binding that cannot be reassigned.
explanation: A const declaration must be initialized where it is declared, and the name can never be pointed at a different value afterward. It is block-scoped. const protects the binding, not the value: an object or array declared with const can still have its contents changed.

examples.title: Declare a constant
examples.explanation: The binding is declared once and its value is printed.

examples.title: Reassignment throws
examples.explanation: Assigning to a const binding throws a TypeError, which the catch block reports.

examples.title: Contents can still change
examples.explanation: The binding still points at the same object; only a property inside it changed.

commonMistakes: Trying to reassign a const binding.
Assuming const makes an object or array deeply immutable.
Declaring a const without an initial value, which is a SyntaxError.

title: let declarations
summary: Declares a block-scoped variable that can be reassigned.
explanation: Use let for values that change over time, such as counters. A let variable exists only inside the block where it is declared, and a block can declare its own variable with the same name as an outer one without affecting it. Reading a let variable before its declaration line runs throws a ReferenceError.

examples.title: Reassign a variable
examples.explanation: A let variable can be given a new value after it is declared.

examples.title: Block scope
examples.explanation: The inner x only exists inside the braces, so the outer x is untouched.

commonMistakes: Declaring the same name twice with let in the same scope, which is a SyntaxError.
Using a let variable before its declaration, which throws a ReferenceError.
Using let for values that never change, where const communicates intent better.

title: Primitive and reference values
summary: Primitives are copied by value; objects are shared by reference.
explanation: Numbers, strings, booleans and other primitives are copied when assigned, so each variable holds its own value. Objects, arrays and functions are stored by reference: assigning one to another variable makes both names point at the same object. Comparing objects with === asks whether they are the same object, not whether they look alike.

examples.title: Primitives are copied
examples.explanation: Changing b does not affect a because b received its own copy of the number.

examples.title: Objects are shared
examples.explanation: first and second point at the same object, so a change through one is visible through the other.

examples.title: Equality compares identity
examples.explanation: p and q have the same contents but are two separate objects.

commonMistakes: Expecting assignment to copy an object, then being surprised when the original changes.
Comparing two objects or arrays with === and expecting a content comparison.

title: Basic operators
summary: Arithmetic and comparison operators, and why === is preferred over ==.
explanation: The arithmetic operators are +, -, *, /, % (remainder) and ** (exponent). === compares value and type with no conversion, while == converts types first, which can produce surprising results. The + operator also joins strings, so mixing a string and a number turns the number into text, whereas - always converts to numbers.
syntax: a + b, a % b, a ** b, a === b

examples.title: Strict vs loose equality
examples.explanation: === sees different types and says false; == converts the string to a number first.

examples.title: Plus with a string
examples.explanation: + joins the text '5' and '3'; - converts '5' to the number 5 and subtracts.

commonMistakes: Using == and being surprised by type conversion; prefer ===.
Adding a string and a number and getting joined text instead of a sum.
